strengths: Combines two well-established variance reduction ideas (Stein-based control functionals and multilevel Monte Carlo) in a natural and technically coherent way, avoiding the domain-specific restrictions of prior multilevel control variate methods (e.g., Nobile & Tesei, Fairbanks et al., Geraci et al.) and the kernel/distribution restrictions of multilevel Bayesian quadrature.

Provides a formal unbiasedness proof (Proposition 1) and a variance upper bound (Theorem 2) that relates the convergence rate to smoothness of the integrand/density and dimensionality, giving some theoretical grounding for the claimed benefits.

The method is simple to implement and does not require expert knowledge of the underlying physical/differential-equation model, which is a genuine practical advantage over some existing multifidelity control variate approaches.

Includes two illustrative experiments (a boundary-value ODE and Bayesian inference for a real-world Lotka-Volterra ecological dataset) where MLCF outperforms MLMC and standard CF baselines under matched computational budgets.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly describes itself as unfinished ('In this initial work...In the full version of this paper we will consider the optimal sample size...'), indicating the work is preliminary and the central practical question of how to allocate samples across levels (crucial for MLMC-type methods) is left unresolved.

The experimental evaluation is very limited: only two low-dimensional examples, no systematic study of how performance degrades with dimension d (despite the paper's own theory predicting rate decay with d), few repetitions (100 and 50), and only three budget points shown as boxplots without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing.

No comparison against the closely related and directly relevant Multilevel Bayesian Quadrature (Li et al. 2023) baseline, despite this being the most comparable existing method discussed at length in the introduction; omitting it undermines the empirical claim of general superiority.

Key assumptions underlying Theorem 2 (rectangular domain X1, boundary vanishing condition A5, high-order smoothness of kernels/densities) are acknowledged in the appendix to not hold in the actual experiments, weakening the connection between the theoretical results and the empirical demonstrations.

The O(m^3) cost of control functionals and the added complexity/cost of tuning kernels and hyperparameters per level is dismissed with a brief unsubstantiated claim that it is negligible, without empirical wall-clock breakdowns supporting this for larger-scale or higher-dimensional problems.

The paper is very short (5 pages main text) with limited discussion of hyperparameter selection (kernel choice, bandwidth, m_l vs n_l split), sensitivity analysis, and no ablation isolating the individual contributions of the control-functional and multilevel components.

Minor clarity/notation issues remain (e.g., inconsistent super/subscripts in Proposition 1, typos such as 'Baysian', unclear justification for why X1_l are treated i.i.d. when samples may come from MCMC), which could confuse readers attempting to reproduce the method.

strengths: The core idea—embedding non-parametric Stein-based control functionals within each level increment of the MLMC telescoping sum—is a natural, well-motivated extension that removes some restrictive assumptions of prior multilevel control-variate work (e.g., specific kernel-density pairs required by Multilevel Bayesian Quadrature, or expert-designed surrogate models required by Nobile & Tesei, Fairbanks et al., Geraci et al.).

The method is broadly applicable: it works with unnormalized densities (important for Bayesian inference), does not require problem-specific expert knowledge, and is compatible with arbitrary sampling designs (IID, QMC, LHS, MCMC).

The paper provides a rigorous unbiasedness proof (Proposition 1) and a variance upper bound (Theorem 2) building on established Stein-kernel convergence theory (Oates et al. 2019), giving some theoretical grounding for the claimed faster convergence rate under smoothness and low-dimensionality assumptions.

Empirical evaluation includes a real-world dataset (Hewitt's snowshoe hare / lynx population data) for the Lotka-Volterra Bayesian inference example, which adds some practical relevance beyond purely synthetic benchmarks.
Reasonable baseline comparisons are included (MLMC, CF, MCMC, MLMCMC) under matched computational budgets, and results consistently favor MLCF in the reported settings.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly frames itself as incomplete/preliminary work: the conclusion states 'In this initial work...' and defers key aspects (optimal sample-size allocation across levels, and an example demonstrating it) to a 'full version of this paper.' This is a strong signal the work is not yet complete for a top-tier venue, and the current experiments use MLMC-optimal (not MLCF-optimal) sample sizes, which likely understates or misrepresents the method's true achievable performance.

The empirical evaluation is very limited: only two low-dimensional examples (a 2D ODE and an 8D Lotka-Volterra posterior), each with a single problem instance repeated over random seeds. There is no exploration of scalability with dimension, number of levels, or kernel choice, despite the paper's own theory showing the convergence rate degrades sharply with dimension (curse of dimensionality), which is a central caveat that is not empirically probed.

No direct comparison to the closest related method, Multilevel Bayesian Quadrature (Li et al. 2023), even in a restricted setting where it would be applicable; the paper only asserts its limitations without empirical contrast.

Theoretical contribution is somewhat incremental: Theorem 2 is essentially a direct adaptation/summation of the single-level convergence result from Oates et al. (2019) applied per level, without substantial new theoretical insight into how the multilevel structure interacts with control functional approximation error (e.g., no analysis of optimal level truncation L, no cost-accuracy tradeoff analysis in the MLMC tradition of Giles).

The added computational overhead of solving an O(m^3) linear system at every level (potentially L+1 times) is dismissed briefly as negligible without quantitative justification across the tested range of level counts and sample sizes.

Some assumptions (A1–A8, e.g., bounded rectangular domain, strict smoothness) are acknowledged not to hold in the experiments, undermining the direct applicability of the theoretical guarantees to the reported empirical results.

Statistical reporting is fairly thin—only boxplots over 50–100 repetitions are shown, without explicit variance-reduction factors, confidence intervals, or discussion of how sensitive results are to hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth, level cost ratios, etc.).

Minor writing issues (e.g., 'Baysian' typo, awkward phrasing) and the paper's overall length/structure feel more consistent with a short workshop submission than a full conference paper with comprehensive evaluation.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of Stein-based non-parametric control variates (control functionals) with the multilevel Monte Carlo framework, addressing a clear gap where existing multilevel control variate methods are either problem-specific (PDEs, low-rank representations, simplified physical models) or restricted to specific kernel-distribution pairs (Bayesian quadrature + MLMC).

Solid theoretical contributions: unbiasedness of the MLCF estimator (Prop 3.1), a variance upper bound tied to smoothness of the integrand/density (Thm 3.2), and closed-form optimal sample allocation across levels (Thm 3.3), with all proofs provided in detail in the appendix.

Broad applicability demonstrated across several qualitatively different settings: a controlled synthetic example validating the theoretical optimal sample sizes, a boundary-value ODE/PDE example compatible with experimental design (QMC/LHS), Bayesian inference for an unnormalized posterior (Lotka-Volterra, using real ecological data and MCMC samples), and an extension to variational inference for Bayesian neural networks (MLCFRG).

The extension to variational inference (Proposition 3.4) is a nice practical contribution, providing a simplified recursive gradient update that reduces computational cost from O(d sum_l n_l^3) to O(d n_L^3), making the method more tractable for iterative optimization.
Extensive implementation details are provided (kernel derivatives, hyperparameter selection via marginal likelihood, sample size tables, cost measurements), which aids reproducibility.

Empirical results consistently show MLCF outperforming both plain CF (single fidelity) and plain MLMC under matched computational budgets across all tested examples, supporting the core motivating hypothesis illustrated in Figure 1.
weaknesses: The method's core computational bottleneck (O(m^3) cost from kernel Gram matrix inversion at each level) is only lightly addressed; the paper claims this cost is small relative to integrand evaluation cost, but this may not hold in higher-dimensional or larger-sample settings, and is acknowledged as a limitation without resolution.

The theoretical guarantees (Thm 3.2, 3.3) explicitly require smooth integrands/densities and low-to-moderate dimensionality, yet the paper applies MLCF to Bayesian neural networks with d=392-522 parameters and ReLU (non-smooth) activations, where these assumptions clearly fail; the connection between theory and this high-dimensional, non-smooth empirical setting is not rigorously justified.

Assumption A8 requires quasi-uniform (space-filling) designs for the low-level samples, yet the Lotka-Volterra experiment uses MCMC samples, which generally do not satisfy such fill-distance conditions; this mismatch between theoretical assumptions and empirical practice is not discussed.

The paper explicitly identifies competing multilevel control variate approaches (e.g., Li et al. 2023 multilevel Bayesian quadrature) but does not include them as empirical baselines, instead asserting without strong supporting evidence that implementation for the more complex experiments is 'either very difficult or not feasible.'

Baselines are somewhat narrow: comparisons are largely restricted to MLMC, standard CF, and MC; no comparison is made against alternative modern scalable control variate methods (e.g., neural/parametric or vector-valued control variates cited in related work) that could also be combined with multilevel structure.

Statistical rigor of the empirical comparisons could be strengthened; while boxplots over replications are shown, there is no formal significance testing, and variance/uncertainty in the reported ELBO/log-likelihood curves for the BNN experiments appears substantial, making the claimed improvement somewhat qualitative.

The paper's discussion of when MLCF provably outperforms CF (the BMLCF vs BCF comparison) relies on informal reasoning about which term dominates rather than a rigorous general bound, weakening the strength of the comparative variance-reduction claims.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, which may hinder accessibility; some appendix content (e.g., basic kernel derivative formulas) could be trimmed to make room for a more thorough discussion of limitations and failure cases.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of Stein-based control functionals with the multilevel Monte Carlo framework, filling a genuine gap since prior multilevel control variate methods are typically domain- or PDE-specific while this approach is broadly applicable.

Solid theoretical contributions: unbiasedness proof (Prop 3.1), a variance upper bound showing faster per-level convergence than MLMC under smoothness assumptions (Thm 3.2), and closed-form optimal sample allocation across levels (Thm 3.3), plus a comparison of the resulting bound to standard CF.

Extension to variational inference (MLCFRG) is a nice practical contribution, including a simplified recursive update rule and reduced computational/memory cost analysis relative to a naive multilevel CF gradient estimator.

Diverse empirical validation across four different problem types (synthetic test-bed, boundary-value ODE, Bayesian inference for the Lotka-Volterra ecological model with real data, and Bayesian neural network variational inference), with consistent evidence that MLCF outperforms MLMC, CF, and MC baselines under matched compute budgets.

Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix with full proofs, explicit kernel formulas/derivatives, hyperparameter selection procedures (marginal likelihood, median heuristics), and thorough experimental configuration details (sample sizes, costs, priors).
Ablations on experimental design (QMC/LHS vs IID sampling), kernel choice, and sample-size strategy for the VI experiments strengthen the empirical case.
weaknesses: Theoretical benefits are explicitly limited to smooth integrands/densities and low-to-moderate dimensionality; the paper does not empirically probe how quickly performance degrades in higher dimensions (BNN experiments have hundreds of parameters but do not include a systematic dimensionality study of the theory's predictions).

The method's O(m^3) cost from kernel Gram matrix inversion at each level is acknowledged but only briefly dismissed as "not severe" without empirical wall-clock scaling analysis for larger m or higher-dimensional problems.

Direct empirical comparison to alternative multilevel control variate baselines (e.g., Nobile & Tesei, Fairbanks et al., Geraci et al., Li et al. 2023 multilevel Bayesian quadrature) is absent; the paper argues these are inapplicable/infeasible in its settings rather than demonstrating this, which weakens the competitive positioning claims.

Optimal sample-size allocation (Theorem 3.3) requires RKHS norm estimates that are difficult to obtain in general nonlinear/real-world settings; the paper's practical workaround (data-driven RKHS norm estimation) is only cited, not empirically validated in the harder examples (ODE, Lotka-Volterra, BNN).

BNN experiments use a relatively simple diagonal Gaussian variational family and modest network sizes (392–522 parameters) on a small subsampled dataset, limiting evidence of scalability to realistic large-scale deep learning settings.

The bound comparison between MLCF and CF/MLMC (paragraph after Theorem 3.3) relies on informal case-based reasoning ("if this term increases/decreases rapidly...") rather than a rigorous general condition, leaving some gaps in when MLCF is guaranteed to dominate.

Some experimental setups (e.g., approximating computational cost as inversely proportional to step size in the illustration example) are simplified in ways that may not reflect real computational costs in more complex applications.
